MINING MAFIA

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Mining Sector is under attack by criminal elements crippling an industry that generates close 25% of country's GDP.

Unique Selling Point:
** ILLEGAL MINING LIKE WE"VE NEVER SEEN BEFORE
** GREAT FOOTAGE

Summary:
The South African Mining Sector is under attack by criminal elements ranging from low level zama-zamas, to business forums demanding their cut of projects and jobs, to organised syndicates running illegal mining operations using big scale equipment.

Limberg Mining Company has been taken over by group of illegal miners who illegally mine and sell chrome they have no mining rights to.

They are a law unto themselves. Despite two police raids and confiscated equipment and commodities valued at just over R13 million - these brazen continue mining illegally - day in and day out.

We investigate the driving forces and ask what the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy is doing to curb this blatant criminality targeting the mining sector.

Further information:
In 2019, the Minerals Council saw a significant number of armed attacks on precious metals facilities by heavily armed gangs. In 2020 that slowed down considerably as the sector and the security establishment got on top of that particular challenge. But with this new trend of illegal operators masquerading as legitimate operators, intervention is desperately needed.

DOES IT HAVE AN IMPACT ON INVESTMENT?
The Minerals Council says YES! it’s an issue. There are calls for a dedicated police unit that has the skills to deal with mining-related policing issues. We must differentiate as an industry between genuine community representation and genuine community concerns — which are very, very real — and this mafia-like behaviour that we’ve seen surrounding procurement in a number of regions around the country.

Social unrest has long bedevilled the sector and has been linked to community grievances, which in many cases have been genuine. But beneath the surface there is also often competition for the spoils, and the industry is starting to label the ringleaders as a mafia.

COMMUNITY IMPACT
The Local Sebilong Community own the land at Zwartskop Farm in Thabazimbi, the Limberg Mining Company have the mining rights from the DMRE. They are fully aware at that the illegal mining operations negatively impacts the wellbeing of the greater community in terms of the legitimate mine's corporate social responsibility initiatives and environmental rehabilitation plans. Community Leader, Frank Tisane is outspoken and points out that the illegal mining operators are causing rifts in the community, there have been threats to those that oppose the criminality and they fear the future of the community should the Limberg Mining Company withdraw as a result of the illegal miners that have essentially hijacked the mine.

THE MINE'S POSITION
Limberg Mining Company has sought legal relief, have called on the DMRE and the police to intervene but they have yet to get control back of the mine. At the same time, the mine has also been issued with a SEction 93 that halts all mining operations - it is believed to stem from unsubstantiated claims made disgruntled community members who felt done in when the dubious contracts were halted. This means that the rightful mining company cannot mine. But while they are in an administrative battle with the DMRE, the illegal mining operation carry on with no regard for the law.

Mining in SOuth AFrica comes with a big price tag if you do it right and lawful way. There are a range of requirements in terms of licenses, environmental impact assessments, community invovlement, etc that needs to accounted for and provided for through the proper channels. Illegal mining operations don't do any of that - so the chrome they steal delivers a much bigger profit margin.

Without the authorities stepping in, there will be no option for legitimate mining companys but to close down and call it day.

As it stands now, as a result of the Section 93, the company has had to retrench close to 400 employees and is currently in business rescue. This as illegal miners continue drive off tonnes and tonnes of stole commodities day in and day out.


FINANCIAL IMPACT
The financial impact of these criminal elements is catastrophic – SA’s mining industry is desperate for foreign investment to maintain operations and open up new opportunities. The constant onslaught of illegal activity and threats to security chases away potential investors, worsening the decline of the industry.

UNDERCOVER ELEMENT
WE contact three of the ringleaders behind some of these illegal mining operations and enquire about buying chrome.

We will try to confront them in Thabazimbi

INTERVIEWS
- MINERALS COUNCIL
- Jono Gay - LIMBERG MINING COMPANY
- Joe van der Walt - SECURITY COMPANY THAT HAS CONNECTED ALL THE DOTS AND IDENTIFIED THE ILLEGAL MINING RINGLEADERS
- Frank Tisane - SEBILONG COMMUNITY CHAIRPERSON
- DMRE LIMPOPO
- UNDERCOVER ELEMENT TO SHOW THAT THE SUSPECTED RINGLEADER ARE DEALING IN CHROME THEY DO NOT OWN

STRUCTURE

VO: The South African Mining Sector is under attack. From low level zama-zamas, to the growing procurement mafia – criminal elements are a law unto themselves and are crippling the country’s mining industry.

LINK: Here in Limpopo, we're not talking about zama zamas, we're talking about what appears to be illegal mining on another level, using big machinery and big money.

VO: These groups are organised and they are brazen. Looking at this exclusive drone footage, it seems like a proper mining operation – with labourers, excavators, rock breaking peckers, TLBs and side tipper trucks running at full steam .

But it isn’t. This mine has been hijacked - opportunistic groups illegally mine and sell chrome, they have no legal mining rights to .

JOE: At one stage, we, // counted // 15 to 20 trucks transporting illegal chrome out of here. We had in the vicinity of 20 to 30 excavators// actually operating in the mining area illegally.

VO: The Limberg Mining Company holds the legal mining rights over this area outside of Thabazimbi in Limpopo. But in August 2020, the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy, or DMRE, issued a Section 93 Directive forcing the company to stop mining. Jono Gay is the CEO of the company.

JONO: The Section 93 was issued where the DMRE through their inspectors came to site, and they believe that a third party was mining on the mining right for its own benefit, which is categorically not the case.

VO: The third party confusion appears to have stemmed from the company’s name change.

LINK: All Limburg mining company operations have been halted by the department, yet a day in and day out mining activities are on the go.

VO: This administrative battle opened the door to criminal syndicates masquerading as legitimate mining operators .

JOE: // they would actually put up huts which which security guards//they would actually use fencing // or demarcate the area for themselves,// Even going as far as falsifying paperwork from the DMR

Security Consultant Joe van der Walt, leads the intelligence driven investigation. Making use of drones, data is analysed to profile the network of suspects and equipment used on site.

The stolen commodities have been traced to buyers in the Asian Market .

DEREK: HOW MAKEI It's sort of legitimate market.
JOE: // a legal product mixed with illegal product, and that's how you legitimize that
DEREK. And it's not sold at market price.
JOE: No, it's sold that discounted prices and in some cases, which we have found that it is sometimes less than 50 to 60 percent of what the market prices is.

VO: While the global demand for chrome fuels black market trading, the South African economy will bare the brunt of this criminality.

JONO: A compliant mine is is healthy contributor to the South African economy where illegal mining is is not contributing at all.

LINK: For the legal mining houses, profits are curtailed because of the costs of compliance for those flouting the law once they've rented the equipment and paid the rock pickers. It's virtually money in the bank.

TEBELLO: it is really economic sabotage for the country, they are really undermining the country's ability to recover and grow

VO: Tebello Chabana, from the Minerals Council of South Africa is clear - illegal mining activity should not be taken lightly.

TEBELLO: the country is losing out on revenues from taxes and royalties. The environment is being degraded through ruthless extraction of minerals by the illegal miners. //. The syndicates have a stranglehold // So it is having a massive impact. // every South African should actually be worried.

VO: The extent of the illegal mining on the ground is simply astonishing. Van der Walt took us to one of the affected areas.

JOE: You know, they have their own geologists
DEREK: You serious geologists.
JOE: Yah! they do!

VO: As we moved in with security, many of the rock pickers scattered, while others carried on with their work not even slightly bothered by the cameras.

DEEREK: Do you know that this is an illegal mining operation?
BUSHIE: Yah they told us.

LINK: They collect what they simply call chrome like this place in heaps and for each heap, they get a thousand rands. And for this community, that's a lot of money.

VO: Beneath the surface, there is competition for the spoils, with infighting and factions raging, explains community leader Frank Tisane.

DEREK: Has there been intimidation or threats leveled at those in the community?
FRANK: Very much so. // people will tell you that will bury you alive//. M6 /// if you are against illegal mining, obviously you are against somebody who will think that you are putting sand on his plate whilst you want things to be done in a, in a, you know, correct manner.

VO: Tisane believes, the vast majority of the already impoverished community are financially disadvantaged by the illegal mining, with very few benefiting.

FRANK: Nothing has been done for the community // we could not insist on getting that money because those proceeds of crime will be seen as people who were encouraging crime.

VO: It’s evident, this is not a formally planned mining operation looking at the environmental impact. Van der Walt explained DMRE officials have been to the site and are aware of the illegal activity.

DEREK: JOE this is a GROOT GAT with its own dangers, I would think.
JOE: the yellow machines can't get in everywhere. So this is where the rock pickers come in because it's easier for them to move in between it, but then gets the whole problem of walls that can possibly cave in and you're looking at possible loss of life. How is that acceptable?

LINK: // the rock pickers do the hard work and as you can see, they're quite blatant. But the top dogs, the traders who make the big bucks are rarely seen and virtually never caught.

TEBELLO: it's illegal activity happening in a clandestine manner, predominantly and so that by its nature,// clearly is a lot of extortion corruption taking place, you know, the bribing of officials, the bribing or threatening of mine personnel.they are syndicates driving these things local and international syndicates. They are organized and they are ruthless.

VO: Illegal mining continues relentlessly with little intervention from local police and the DMRE.

JONO: T-hey are not supportive enough specifically of junior miners. We simply just do not have the scale to deal with the extent of illegal mining that that we're currently dealing with. And I think we are not the only ones in this position.

VO: The DMRE’s Director for Criminal Enforcement, Advocate Shadrack Nkuna, disagrees.

SHADARCK: We are working very hard to ensure that we eliminate the problem of illegal mining in our country.
DEREK: It just seems you've got a long way to go.
SHADARCK: Well, there is a lot of work to be done that I agree, but it is something that eventually we are going to win. M16

VO: But the Limberg Mining Company has only lost. In the year that the Section 93 halted operations - the company has gone into business rescue and has had to retrench close to 400 employees - while illegal miner operate unabated.

But just hours before our interview, low and behold, the DMRE lifted this year long Section 93.

DEREK: Is that coincidental?
SHADARCK: I ….that is. I cannot say coincidentally or not. Our position is there is a pending litigation between Limberg and the department, but hence
DEREK: so we're giving you breaking news
SHADARCK: not necessarily that, necessarily breaking news...

VO: Advocate Nkuna had no knowledge of the upliftment and declined to comment further on the matter.

Back on the mine, we discovered a rock breaking pecker in full swing. At the site, two men claiming to be mechanics were not happy with the cameras and scurried off.

LINK: A machine like this, making noise like this, digging a crater of this size, and the dept - what are they doing about it?

VO: The self-proclaimed mechanics phoned the man allegedly in charge - Prince Manyama.

DEREK: ….but you don't have any mining rights
PRINCE:Sir, your allegations are unfounded.// Sir, come to Northam – I will present all the necessary proof.
DEREK: the proof we want is that you //have a mining right.
PRINCE:I will provide you…. YOU WANT.

VO: Manyama in turn requested that we bring proof of Limberg Mining Company’s mining rights. We showed him and his colleague the document as we set up.

DEREK: When we spoke to each other on the phone, you said that you would bring your mining right?// Can I see it?
MANYANA: I can't produce such a sensitive documents for the media //
DEREK: now it's a secret document?
MANYAMA: No, no, no, no. I'm not saying it's a secret document. I'm saying it's a private in a way that I don't know what you want to do with it. For starters,
DEREK: we just want proof.
MANYAMA: then I'm telling you, if you want proof that I do hold a mining permit, you can go and verify with the DMRE.

VO: He refused to give any specific information and insisted his name would suffice with the DMRE .

MANYAMA: Sir, I feel like you're antagonizing me.
DEREK: I feel you're not answering my questions.

VO: Manyama claimed he was working in his demarcated area . While we saw this area, the machine was not in that fenced location.

MANYAMA: Then, it’s not my area, my area is well demarcated .

VO: He implied maybe those weren’t his workers.

DEREK: //the mechanics gave us your number they’re repairing your machine? MANYAMA: OK. But but but but but I find I find the whole, the whole assertions and the whole interview being a fallacy now

VO: The DMRE was able to find records for Motsiri Prince Manyama.

SHADARCK: Mr Manyama is mining illegally in the sense that he had a mining permit that was issued to him by the department, but simply because he could not comply with the terms and conditions attached to that mining permit. It has since been suspended. M9
DEREK: Are you going to take action against him now?
SHADARCK: Obviously, we will have to take action against him because he's mining illegally.

VO: We put this to Manyama - but he didn’t reply.

Interestingly, this wasn’t Manyama’s first run in with authorities. A court order issued in January 2020, against Manyama ordered him and other illegal miners, to cease and desist from mining activity, on the company’s mining area .

JONO: //it has been a tremendous battle. We are incurring extensive costs, having to deal with security, to try and remove illegal miners.

VO: Van der Walt praised an external Hawks team that carried out two raids this year which resulted in confiscated equipment and commodities worth millions of rands and at least 20 arrests.

DEREK: So roughly, what's the value of all this heavy duty equipment?
JOE: Taking into account a product// most probably looking at close to 18 million // The only problem is that it hasn't stopped

VO: But the destruction and the damage goes beyond Limberg Mining Company - it requires urgent and decisive action.

TEBELLO: These trends are having quite a big impact, // definitely having a negative impact on the perception of South Africa as a, you know, mining destination. M10// I mean, who's going to want to invest in a lawless country? M9

VO: Criminal elements running full scale mining operations are crippling the mining sector by illegally mining and selling chrome, they have no mining rights to.

TEBELLO: It is really economic sabotage for the country. they are really undermining the country's ability to recover and grow

VO: We investigate the driving forces behind this blatant criminality targeting the mining sector.

VO: Illegal mining targets a chrome mine in Limpopo – day in and day out the criminal activity carries on unabated.

JOE: We had in the vicinity of 20 to 30 excavators// actually operating in the mining area illegally.

VO: We investigate the lucrative business of high stakes illegal mining.


PROMO 3 – 11 SEC
VO: There are tensions brewing in Limpopo - as criminal networks take over lucrative mines with next level illegal operations – mining commodities they have no legal claim to.

metadata.Summary: The South African Mining Sector is under attack by criminal elements ranging from low level zama-zamas, to business forums demanding their cut of projects and jobs, to organised syndicates running illegal mining operations using big scale equipment. Limberg Mining Company has been taken over by group of illegal miners who illegally mine and sell chrome they have no mining rights to. They are a law unto themselves. Despite two police raids and confiscated equipment and commodities valued at just over R13 million - these brazen continue mining illegally - day in and day out. We investigate the driving forces and ask what the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy is doing to curb this blatant criminality targeting the mining sector.
metadata.Further information: In 2019, the Minerals Council saw a significant number of armed attacks on precious metals facilities by heavily armed gangs. In 2020 that slowed down considerably as the sector and the security establishment got on top of that particular challenge. But with this new trend of illegal operators masquerading as legitimate operators, intervention is desperately needed. DOES IT HAVE AN IMPACT ON INVESTMENT? The Minerals Council says YES! it’s an issue. There are calls for a dedicated police unit that has the skills to deal with mining-related policing issues. We must differentiate as an industry between genuine community representation and genuine community concerns — which are very, very real — and this mafia-like behaviour that we’ve seen surrounding procurement in a number of regions around the country. Social unrest has long bedevilled the sector and has been linked to community grievances, which in many cases have been genuine. But beneath the surface there is also often competition for the spoils, and the industry is starting to label the ringleaders as a mafia. COMMUNITY IMPACT The Local Sebilong Community own the land at Zwartskop Farm in Thabazimbi, the Limberg Mining Company have the mining rights from the DMRE. They are fully aware at that the illegal mining operations negatively impacts the wellbeing of the greater community in terms of the legitimate mine's corporate social responsibility initiatives and environmental rehabilitation plans. Community Leader, Frank Tisane is outspoken and points out that the illegal mining operators are causing rifts in the community, there have been threats to those that oppose the criminality and they fear the future of the community should the Limberg Mining Company withdraw as a result of the illegal miners that have essentially hijacked the mine. THE MINE'S POSITION Limberg Mining Company has sought legal relief, have called on the DMRE and the police to intervene but they have yet to get control back of the mine. At the same time, the mine has also been issued with a SEction 93 that halts all mining operations - it is believed to stem from unsubstantiated claims made disgruntled community members who felt done in when the dubious contracts were halted. This means that the rightful mining company cannot mine. But while they are in an administrative battle with the DMRE, the illegal mining operation carry on with no regard for the law. Mining in SOuth AFrica comes with a big price tag if you do it right and lawful way. There are a range of requirements in terms of licenses, environmental impact assessments, community invovlement, etc that needs to accounted for and provided for through the proper channels. Illegal mining operations don't do any of that - so the chrome they steal delivers a much bigger profit margin. Without the authorities stepping in, there will be no option for legitimate mining companys but to close down and call it day. As it stands now, as a result of the Section 93, the company has had to retrench close to 400 employees and is currently in business rescue. This as illegal miners continue drive off tonnes and tonnes of stole commodities day in and day out. FINANCIAL IMPACT The financial impact of these criminal elements is catastrophic – SA’s mining industry is desperate for foreign investment to maintain operations and open up new opportunities. The constant onslaught of illegal activity and threats to security chases away potential investors, worsening the decline of the industry. UNDERCOVER ELEMENT WE contact three of the ringleaders behind some of these illegal mining operations and enquire about buying chrome. We will try to confront them in Thabazimbi INTERVIEWS - MINERALS COUNCIL - Jono Gay - LIMBERG MINING COMPANY - Joe van der Walt - SECURITY COMPANY THAT HAS CONNECTED ALL THE DOTS AND IDENTIFIED THE ILLEGAL MINING RINGLEADERS - Frank Tisane - SEBILONG COMMUNITY CHAIRPERSON - DMRE LIMPOPO - UNDERCOVER ELEMENT TO SHOW THAT THE SUSPECTED RINGLEADER ARE DEALING IN CHROME THEY DO NOT OWN
